summary:
I've been building character-forge, a tool that generates SillyTavern characters through an interview instead of a one-shot prompt: it asks questions, drafts a brief, builds the fields, then audits its own output before you're allowed to commit it. I spent time on market research before writing any more README copy — turns out the closest competitor sits at 157 stars and does none of this (no interview, no lorebook authoring), and a second small project independently converged on the same phased design, which was a useful gut check that the shape is right.

Most of the actual engineering was fixing things that broke live. Lore entries generated by the tool were "keyword-triggered," meaning they'd shift position in the prompt turn to turn and force a full context reprocess on the model serving it — every RP turn was re-reading the whole conversation from scratch. Making those entries always-inject fixed it, but the fix had to be applied in two separate places (the card file and a linked lore file) and then patched again after I found it only survives if you hard-refresh the browser before the next save, or a stale in-memory copy silently reverts it. Also had a build step that would quietly reinvent a character's whole backstory from an empty chat log and overwrite the saved version — traced it, added a guard so it only rebuilds from what was actually saved.

On the side, I set up a git workflow for contributing to a friend's open-source project (a tabletop VTT app) without being able to push to his repo directly — private working repo, a read-only mirror of his main branch, and a public fork just for opening PRs. The one rule that matters there: never commit to the branch that mirrors his, or every sync turns into a conflict.

highlights.oneLiner: Interview-driven SillyTavern character generator with self-audit before commit
